title: Appassimento
subtitle: Drying the grapes
objectives: Explain how drying changes the grape

steps.title: Drying for months
steps.body: Appassimento is the drying of grapes after harvest. Healthy, loose bunches are picked by hand and laid on bamboo racks or plastic crates in airy lofts, called fruttai. They dry for about 100 to 120 days, losing 30 to 40% of their weight. Sugar, acid and flavour concentrate.
steps.highlight: Three to four months in fruttai

steps.title: Not just water loss
steps.body: Drying is a living process. The berries keep metabolising, changing their chemistry. Some acids decrease, glycerol rises, and new aromas form. Resveratrol and other compounds increase. A little noble rot sometimes develops, adding complexity. The result is dried cherry, raisin and spice flavours.
steps.highlight: Grapes keep living as they dry

steps.prompt: How much weight do grapes typically lose during appassimento?
steps.explanation: About a third, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour.

steps.title: Modern fruttai
steps.body: Traditionally, grapes dried in attics with open windows, at the mercy of the weather. Today many fruttai have fans and dehumidifiers to control conditions and prevent grey rot. Some producers argue that natural drying gives more complexity; others prefer control. Both are allowed.

steps.explanation: Fermentation happens after drying, not during.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Appassimento dries grapes for three to four months
Berries lose 30 to 40% of their weight and change chemically
Modern lofts control humidity to prevent rot
